text: Hey, welcome back to the studio.
Today we're making soy candles at home, and it's easier than it looks.
A lot of you asked me, what if the wax gets too hot, or the candle comes out lumpy?
Honestly, I was scared of it too the first time.
But with a thermometer, a steady pour and a little patience, it's one of the most beginner friendly crafts out there.
Everything we need today comes in the Pour Kit.
Soy wax flakes, cotton wicks, a pouring pitcher, a thermometer and four fragrance oils.
Before we start, a quick word on safety.
Always melt the wax in a double boiler, never directly on the burner.
Keep the handle dry, keep kids and pets away from the stove, and never leave melting wax alone.
First project, a classic jar candle.
Fill the pitcher about halfway with wax flakes and set it inside a pot of simmering water.
Stir gently until everything is clear and the thermometer reads 85 degrees.
While it melts, stick a wick to the bottom of the jar and center it with the wooden clip.
Now take the pitcher off the heat and add the fragrance oil, about 10% of the wax weight.
Stir slowly for two full minutes, so the scent really binds with the wax.
Let it cool down to 60 degrees and pour in one steady stream.
Leave about a centimeter at the top and let it set for four hours.
That's it!
Look at that smooth, creamy top.
Simple, right? And the whole room already smells like vanilla.
Next, let's make something you can give away.
A two-tone candle, poured in layers.
I'm adding a few chips of terracotta dye to the bottom layer and leaving the top one natural.
Pour the first layer, then wait about 30 minutes until the surface is firm but still warm.
If the timing feels too hard, just touch the surface: it should feel like soft butter.
Now the natural layer goes on top, nice and slow, over the back of a spoon.
The line between the two colors turned out perfectly straight.
A ribbon and a handwritten tag, and it's ready to wrap.
For the last idea, let's give an old teacup a second life.
This one was hiding in the back of my cupboard with a chip on the rim.
Same wax, same wick, just a smaller pour.
Here, a few bumps on top are part of the charm.
Mismatched cups make the best candles anyway.
Once all three are set, let them cure for 48 hours before you light them.
Trim each wick to about six millimeters, and now it lights up.
And here they are, our three finished candles.
Anyone can make these in one evening with the Pour Kit.
And the same method works for almost any container.
Tins, teacups, coconut shells, even an old sugar bowl.
So, still afraid of hot wax?
Tell us in the comments which scent we should try next.
And subscribe to keep your next weekend project easy.
Happy pouring!
